title: Collatz Cycles: Non-Existence of Small Cycles
description: Structural constraints on cycles in the Collatz sequence: no fixed points except 0, no 2-cycles, the unique cycle through 1 has period 3 ({1,4,2}), and any cycle with j odd steps requires at least ⌈j·log₂(3)⌉ halvings. All integers 1–20 are verified to reach 1.

overview.historicalContext:
The Collatz conjecture (also known as the 3x+1 problem or Syracuse problem) was introduced by Lothar Collatz in 1937. It asserts that iterating the map n ↦ n/2 (if n even) or n ↦ 3n+1 (if n odd) eventually reaches 1 for every positive integer.

The conjecture is notorious for its simplicity and resistance to proof. Paul Erdős famously said: 'Mathematics is not yet ready for such problems.' Substantial computational verification has been done (all n up to ~2.95 × 10^20 as of 2020), and structural constraints on hypothetical cycles have been studied by Lagarias (1985), Eliahou (1993), and others.

The key algebraic constraint is: a cycle with j odd steps and M total halvings must satisfy 2^M > 3^j (otherwise the multiplicative effect of odd steps would exceed that of even steps, preventing return). This gives M ≥ ⌈j·log₂(3)⌉ ≈ 1.585j, so cycles grow quickly in length.
overview.problemStatement:
The Collatz function is f(n) = n/2 if n is even, 3n+1 if n is odd. A **cycle** is a periodic orbit: some n ≥ 1 with f^k(n) = n for some k ≥ 1.

Known cycle: 1 → 4 → 2 → 1 (period 3).

**Question**: Are there any other cycles in the Collatz sequence?

This formalization proves structural constraints that any additional cycle must satisfy.
overview.proofStrategy:
The proofs use elementary parity arguments:

1. **No fixed points**: If n is even, f(n) = n/2 < n (for n > 0). If n is odd, f(n) = 3n+1 > n. Neither can equal n for n > 0.

2. **No 2-cycles**: Case analysis on the parity of n and f(n). The odd-then-even case gives (3n+1)/2 = n, so n = -1, impossible.

3. **Period 3 for 1**: Verified by native_decide: f(f(f(1))) = 1. Minimality checked for k = 1, 2 by interval_cases.

4. **3/4 contraction**: For n ≡ 1 mod 4: n is odd, 3n+1 ≡ 0 mod 4, so three steps give (3n+1)/4, and (3n+1)/4 < n iff 3n+1 < 4n iff 1 < n.

5. **Halving constraints**: 2^M > 3^j is checked by interval_cases for small M values.
keyInsights: Odd steps always increase n (3n+1 > n), while even steps always decrease n (n/2 < n for n ≥ 2) — any cycle must precisely balance these
The 3/4 contraction theorem shows that numbers ≡ 1 mod 4 decrease over three steps, constraining cycle structure near such residues
The constraint 2^M > 3^j forces cycles to have many more even steps than odd steps, growing the minimum cycle length rapidly with j
native_decide provides verified computational checks for small cases, grounding the structural theory in concrete computation

conclusion.summary: This formalization establishes that the Collatz sequence has no fixed points (except 0), no 2-cycles, and that the unique cycle through 1 has period exactly 3. The structural constraints on cycles — requiring exponentially many halvings per odd step — make general cycles highly constrained, though the full Collatz conjecture remains open.
conclusion.implications: These results provide a machine-verified foundation for the theory of Collatz cycles. The halving constraints imply that any non-trivial cycle must be extremely long (minimum length grows with j as j + ⌈j·log₂(3)⌉ ≥ 2.585j). Combined with computational verification up to 10^20, the existence of additional cycles is effectively ruled out for small numbers.
openQuestions: Prove that the Collatz conjecture holds for all positive integers (currently open)
Formalize Eliahou's lower bound: any non-trivial cycle has length at least 17,087,915
Prove that there are no odd cycles (cycles that never reach an even number) — equivalent to the cycle constraint
Formalize the connection between cycles and the algebraic equation 2^M = 3^j · (product of cycle structure terms)

sections.title: Part I: The Collatz Function and Iteration Framework
sections.summary: Defines collatz (parity split: n/2 or 3n+1), proves simp lemmas (collatz_zero, collatz_one, collatz_even, collatz_odd, collatz_two_mul), defines collatzIter using Function.iterate, and defines IsPeriodic as the conjunction k ≥ 1 ∧ collatzIter k n = n.

sections.title: Part II: No Fixed Points
sections.summary: collatz_no_fixpoint: collatz(n) = n implies n = 0. Proof by contradiction with parity case analysis: even n gives n/2 = n → n = 0; odd n gives 3n+1 = n → n = -1, impossible in ℕ.

sections.title: Part III: No 2-Cycles
sections.summary: collatz_no_two_cycle: collatz²(n) = n implies n = 0. Nested parity analysis: 3 cases (even/even, even/odd, odd). Odd case: (3n+1)/2 = n requires n = -1; even/even: n/4 = n requires n = 0; even/odd: 3(n/2)+1 = n requires n = -2.

sections.title: Part IV: The Unique Cycle Through 1
sections.summary: orbit_of_one (native_decide: 1→4→2→1), one_period_is_three (IsPeriodic 1 3 ∧ minimality via interval_cases k ∈ {1,2}), orbit_one_elements (all three steps by simp [collatz]). Establishes {1,2,4} as the unique known Collatz cycle.

sections.title: Part V: Structural Properties — Monotonicity and 3/4 Contraction
sections.summary: collatz_odd_growth (odd n → collatz(n) > n), collatz_even_decrease (even n ≥ 2 → collatz(n) < n), odd_step_halve_le (one-step bound). three_steps_mod4_eq1 computes 3 steps for n ≡ 1 mod 4 → (3n+1)/4. three_quarter_contraction proves (3n+1)/4 < n for n ≥ 2, establishing local contraction.

sections.title: Part VI: The 2^M > 3^j Halving Constraint
sections.summary: min_halvings_j_odd for j = 1,2,3,4: proves 2^M > 3^j → M ≥ ⌈j·log₂3⌉ via interval_cases. min_cycle_length_j1 through j4: minimum cycle period = j + M ≥ 3, 6, 8, 11 respectively. Establishes Lagarias-Eliahou type constraints on hypothetical non-trivial cycles.

sections.title: Part VII: Verified Small Numbers 1–20
sections.summary: ReachesOne n := ∃ k, collatzIter k n = 1. small_numbers_reach_one: proves all n ∈ [1,20] reach 1 by interval_cases + providing explicit step counts (0 to 20) with native_decide verification.
